So the story finally makes sense and I had an epiphany. The game isn't about the story, it's meant to be looked at from a philosophical standpoint. It all comes together so nicely. The game is meant to be symbolic of the human struggle. Magic is science, Lightning is faith/religion, Dark is humanity's desire (basically to be human), Chaos is strife, and Fire, that which everyone strives for, is life. The overarching theme is the folly of it all.

All of the games have you starting out by not knowing where to go, or really what you're trying to achieve. All you know is that you need to get to the First Flame [life], like in real life, you just know you need to live. Also in reality, you need a purpose to drive you, or else you become just another person [hollow], with no drive. You just exist. Gwyn led the world blindly along a false path by keeping the flame alight [faith] and tried to keep himself above humans [Dark, humanity] to protect the flame [life] and he meant well, but blindly threw himself into it [life] to keep it going. In doing so, as Aldia had said, he kept the illusion going for everyone else. He became a martyr. The serpents want the flame [life] to die, then they can inherit the world [assuming they are immortal, though imperfect]. They just used humans [desire] to achieve their goals. Seath went insane and ultimately achieved only a semblance of his goal [science]. The Witch of Izalith tampered with the flame [life] and created a literal living hell [strife], and Manus completely lost control of his emotions and wrecked everything around him [desire].

In the second game, many years down the line, we see the consequences of many peoples' actions. If we beat the game without doing any DLCs or seeing Aldia, we just blindly go through the game to seek the flame [life] "without really knowing why." Just like a soul just seeking to live just for the sake of living, but having no real impact on the world for the better, you just keep it going. However, by doing the DLCs and talking with Aldia, you realize the sins of past kings, and what their lack of foresight has done, and how you must not repeat the same mistakes if you want to beat the curse. The curse is being human and our folly and missteps shaping our world. We mean well, but we must educate ourselves to truly make the world a better place.

The theme of DS2 is about how many people have tried solving the world's problems in many different ways, but failed. The Chosen Undead's choice didn't matter, as either solution (letting the Dark take over in the hands of the Serpents or lighting the fire) were ineffectual. He was just doing as he was told by someone else (Frampt) and played into someone elses' hands when he deviated (Kaathe). As proof, Vendrick tried doing what we did in the first game, to no effect, and lighting the fire just leads to another case of the curse. Shulva tried keeping to themselves, were religious [faith] and banned magic [science], and fell. The Old Iron king tried seeking power and riches [desire, humanity], and ended up ruining himself and everything around him [chaos]. The Ivory king tried facing his problems with force [chaos], head on, and only ended up becoming part of the Chaos himself, even though he meant well. Aldia tried experimenting [science] and tossing aside his morality [humanity], only to solve nothing. Vendrick tried blindly listening to someone [Nashandra, faith], running from his problems, locking things away, and yet, still, has not solved anything.

Yet we, after experiencing the "sins of our fathers" now are educated and can go into our future and perhaps make the world a better place by trying something else. We reach our destination and are put to the test. Those put in place by Vendrick, the Throne Defender [faith, Lightning] and Throne Watcher [science, Magic] stand in our way. We prove that we have power over both and are confronted by Nashandra [humanity's errors and desires, Dark] and prove that we can overcome them. Without those in the way we are faced with a final challenge, Aldia, who had no faith, tossed away his humanity and was failed by science [strife, Chaos]. Throughout the story he tries to test your resolve. You end up showing you have the power to beat that as well, and become a true monarch, fit to lead the world [facing life]. This time, you are presented with a choice. You can knowingly continue the illusion, or become yet another one to try a new way, without repeating past mistakes. "Light, Dark, or something else entirely..." After hearing Aldia's parting words, you clench your fist, unshaken in your decision, and press on. This is the human struggle. Dark Souls 1 and 2 was just one gigantic life lesson. That was the true meaning of Dark Souls and the true final ending. Such is life. Bravo From. Brav-fucking-O.

And as an add-on story-wise, you have the power of past kings to prevent you from hollowing (crowns), yet utilizing the curse to prevent yourself from dying. You've now got the knowledge of past sins, the power to do more, your morality intact, and the faith to press on. You will do better.
